ports.where: File transfer without encryption. Rare at home today.
Encrypted remote command line. Should not be opened to the internet in a router’s port forwarding without need.
Unencrypted remote command line. A router or printer that offers it to the internet is a risk.
Mail transfer between mail servers. Mail apps send through 587 or 465 instead.
DNS lookups. If a filter or firewall blocks it, websites fail by name while a ping to a numeric address still gets replies.
How a device gets its address from the router (the router listens on 67, the device on 68). An address starting with 169.254 means this exchange failed.
The device’s side of the address assignment (see port 67).
Web pages without encryption (HTTP).
Fetching mail without encryption (POP3); 995 is the encrypted form.
Clock synchronisation. A device with a wrong clock shows certificate warnings on correct websites.
Name lookup of older Windows file and printer sharing in the local network.
Part of older Windows file and printer sharing in the local network.
Older Windows file and printer sharing in the local network.
Reading mail (IMAP); 993 is the encrypted form mail apps normally use.
Network management. Many network printers report their status over it.
Encrypted web pages (HTTPS) – almost every website. If 443 works and a site still fails, the fault is not a blocked port.
Windows file and printer sharing (SMB) in the local network. Should never be forwarded from the internet to a PC.
Sending mail with encryption from the start – one of the two numbers a mail app asks for under “outgoing server”.
Key exchange for IPsec VPNs. If a hotel or guest network blocks it, such a VPN cannot connect.
The older LPD way of sending print jobs to a network printer.
The device’s side of IPv6 address assignment (DHCPv6).
The router’s side of IPv6 address assignment (DHCPv6).
Sending mail from a mail app (“outgoing server”, with STARTTLS).

Internet Printing Protocol – the way current operating systems talk to network printers, including driverless printing. If the printer sits in another network, for example the guest Wi-Fi, the computer cannot reach it on this port.

Internet Printing Protocol – the way current operating systems talk to network printers, including driverless printing. If the printer sits in another network, for example the guest Wi-Fi, the computer cannot reach it on this port.

ports.desc: DNS query-response protocol run over TLS
ports.where: Encrypted DNS (DNS over TLS). Networks that block it break a fixed “Private DNS” provider on a phone.
Reading mail with encryption (IMAP) – the “incoming server” port in most mail apps.
Fetching mail with encryption (POP3).
OpenVPN’s registered port.
Device discovery in the local network (UPnP). Lets PCs find routers, TVs and some printers.
Remote Desktop. A caller who asks you to turn on remote access or to forward this port is not support.

ports.desc: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN) port
ports.where: Helps voice and video calls find a path through the router (STUN).
Windows’ discovery of network printers and scanners (WSD).
IPsec VPN traffic through a router (NAT traversal).

Multicast DNS: how devices find printers and each other by name in the local network without any setup. On a network that keeps devices apart from each other (guest Wi-Fi, “client isolation”), these messages do not get through and printers are not found automatically.
Windows’ name lookup for devices in the local network when no DNS server knows them.
A common second port for web pages, for example a device’s settings page.
Raw print data straight to the printer. Windows’ “Standard TCP/IP Port” for printers uses it by default.

wu.name: WU_E_PT_HTTP_STATUS_NOT_FOUND
wu.meaning: The update server did not find the requested file (the web’s status 404).
wu.next: Wait and retry later; the fault is at the server or with an outdated update list. Only if it lasts for days, reset the update cache as in our guide.

wu.name: WU_E_PT_HTTP_STATUS_PROXY_AUTH_REQ
wu.meaning: A proxy server between the PC and Microsoft demands a sign-in the update service cannot give.
wu.next: On a home PC, check whether a proxy is set in the network settings or by a VPN or filter app, and switch it off for a test. On a work PC, ask IT.

wu.name: WU_E_PT_HTTP_STATUS_SERVICE_UNAVAIL
wu.meaning: The update server answered that it is overloaded or unavailable (the web’s status 503).
wu.next: Wait an hour and try again. Nothing on the PC needs fixing. On a work PC the update server belongs to the company – ask IT.

wu.name: WU_E_PT_WINHTTP_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED
wu.meaning: The name of the update server or of a proxy could not be looked up – a DNS or proxy problem, not an update problem.
wu.next: Test whether websites open. If names fail in general, follow the DNS guide; if a proxy is set, switch it off for a test.

wu.name: WU_E_DM_FAILTOCONNECTTOBITS
wu.meaning: The update service could not reach Windows’ background download service (BITS).
wu.next: Restart the PC, which restarts that service, and try again. The Windows troubleshooter in our guide checks these services.

wu.name: WU_E_UH_INVALIDMETADATA
wu.meaning: The description data of an update is unusable.
wu.next: Microsoft’s remedy is to make Windows download everything fresh by renaming the update cache folders – the last step in our guide, with the undo.

wu.name: WU_E_UH_INSTALLERFAILURE
wu.meaning: The installer of an update reported a failure. The code says only that, not why.
wu.next: Restart and retry, then run Windows’ troubleshooter as in our guide. Note the KB number of the failing update for any search on Microsoft’s site.

wu.name: WU_E_UH_NEEDANOTHERDOWNLOAD
wu.meaning: The downloaded update was unusable and has to be fetched again.
wu.next: Check for updates again – Windows repeats the download by itself. Only if it loops, reset the update cache as in our guide.

wu.name: WU_E_UH_POSTREBOOTSTILLPENDING
wu.meaning: An update is waiting for its restart and blocks the next one until then.
wu.next: Restart the PC (Restart, not Shut down), then check for updates again.

wu.name: InstallFileLocked
wu.meaning: Another program is holding a file the update needs. Microsoft names security software and similar background programs as the usual cause.
wu.next: Restart and start the update before opening anything else. If it repeats, follow Microsoft’s clean-start instructions on the linked page.

wu.name: WU_E_CALL_CANCELLED
wu.meaning: The update run was cancelled – by you, by a shutdown or by the update service itself.
wu.next: Start “Check for updates” again and leave the PC on until it finishes.

wu.name: WU_E_INSTALL_NOT_ALLOWED
wu.meaning: Another installation is still running, or the PC is waiting for a restart.
wu.next: Wait a few minutes or restart the PC, then try again.

wu.name: WU_E_NOT_APPLICABLE
wu.meaning: Windows found that the update does not apply to this PC.
wu.next: Nothing to repair. If you downloaded the update by hand, check the Windows version first.

wu.name: WU_E_SERVICE_STOP
wu.meaning: The update service or Windows was shutting down while the update was at work.
wu.next: Start the PC normally and check for updates again; do not switch off during an update.

wu.name: WU_E_NO_INTERACTIVE_USER
wu.meaning: The update needs someone signed in to finish, and nobody was.
wu.next: Sign in, start the update again and let the PC restart when it asks.

wu.name: WU_E_ALL_UPDATES_FAILED
wu.meaning: Every update in the batch failed. Microsoft’s most common finding is security software blocking Windows’ update folders.
wu.next: Restart and retry. If you use third-party antivirus, check whether it reports blocking Windows Update; then run Windows’ own troubleshooter as in our guide.

wu.name: WU_E_DOWNLOAD_FAILED
wu.meaning: An update could not be downloaded.
wu.next: Check the connection and free disk space, then retry. If the same update keeps failing, reset the update cache as described at the end of our guide.

wu.name: ERROR_SERVICE_DISABLED
wu.meaning: The Windows Update service is switched off or not running, so nothing can be searched or installed.
wu.next: Restart the PC. If the code returns, open the Services app, look for “Windows Update” and check that it is not set to Disabled (needs an administrator). On a work PC this is set by IT.

wu.name: ERROR_FAIL_REBOOT_REQUIRED
wu.meaning: An earlier installation still needs a restart, or a setting keeps Windows’ installer service from starting.
wu.next: Restart the PC (Restart, not Shut down) and try again. On a managed PC the installer setting comes from IT.

wu.name: BG_E_VALIDATION_FAILED
wu.meaning: A download did not arrive as it was sent. Microsoft points to firewalls or filters that alter downloads.
wu.next: Pause a VPN, web filter or third-party firewall for a test and retry, or try another network.

wu.name: TIME_OUT_ERRORS
wu.meaning: The connection to the update server could not be set up or timed out. Microsoft names firewalls and proxies that block its download addresses.
wu.next: Open a website to check the connection. Pause a VPN or proxy and try again; if you can, try another network. If only updates fail for hours, wait – nothing on the PC needs changing.

wu.name: TIME_OUT_ERRORS
wu.meaning: The connection to the update server was cut during the transfer.
wu.next: Open a website to check the connection. Pause a VPN or proxy and try again; if you can, try another network. If only updates fail for hours, wait – nothing on the PC needs changing.

wu.name: ERROR_INVALID_DATA
wu.meaning: A downloaded update file is damaged or incomplete.
wu.next: Restart and let Windows download it again. If the same update fails again, the last step of our guide – resetting the update cache – makes Windows fetch it fresh.

wu.name: USO_E_SERVICE_SHUTTING_DOWN
wu.meaning: The update service shut down in the middle – Microsoft describes this after long idle periods.
wu.next: Keep the PC awake and plugged in, start the update again and stay until the download and installation finish.

wu.name: CBS_E_ABORT
wu.meaning: The installation step took longer than Windows allows and was stopped by its own watchdog.
wu.next: Give the PC time: close other programs, keep it plugged in and try the update again.

wu.name: CBS_E_SOURCE_MISSING
wu.meaning: Windows’ own store of system files is damaged, so the update cannot be put together. Files needed for the update are missing.
wu.next: Restart and try once more. If it returns, Microsoft’s remedy is Windows’ built-in repair (DISM with RestoreHealth, then SFC) from an administrator command prompt – the exact commands are on the linked Microsoft page. Nothing has to be downloaded for it.

wu.name: CBS_E_STORE_CORRUPTION
wu.meaning: Windows’ own store of system files is damaged, so the update cannot be put together.
wu.next: Restart and try once more. If it returns, Microsoft’s remedy is Windows’ built-in repair (DISM with RestoreHealth, then SFC) from an administrator command prompt – the exact commands are on the linked Microsoft page. Nothing has to be downloaded for it.

wu.name: E_ACCESSDENIED
wu.meaning: Windows was refused access to a file or setting it needs for the update.
wu.next: Restart, sign in with an administrator account and retry. If it stays, the cause has to be read from Windows’ update log as Microsoft describes – a job for someone experienced, not for trial and error.

wu.name: ERROR_FILE_CORRUPT
wu.meaning: Windows’ own store of system files is damaged, so the update cannot be put together.
wu.next: Restart and try once more. If it returns, Microsoft’s remedy is Windows’ built-in repair (DISM with RestoreHealth, then SFC) from an administrator command prompt – the exact commands are on the linked Microsoft page. Nothing has to be downloaded for it.

wu.name: ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND
wu.meaning: A folder or file the update expects is not where it should be.
wu.next: Restart and retry. If the same update fails again, reset the update cache as described at the end of our guide.

wu.name: ERROR_SXS_ASSEMBLY_MISSING
wu.meaning: Windows’ own store of system files is damaged, so the update cannot be put together. A part of an earlier update was left half installed.
wu.next: Restart and try once more. If it returns, Microsoft’s remedy is Windows’ built-in repair (DISM with RestoreHealth, then SFC) from an administrator command prompt – the exact commands are on the linked Microsoft page. Nothing has to be downloaded for it.

wu.name: WININET_E_DECODING_FAILED
wu.meaning: The PC could not read what the update server sent; Microsoft traces this to the encryption setup (TLS 1.2) on older systems.
wu.next: Install all other pending updates first and restart. Microsoft’s page names the update that fixes it on old systems; do not change security settings by hand.

wu.name: WININET_E_TIMEOUT
wu.meaning: The PC got no answer from the update server in time.
wu.next: Open a website to check the connection. Pause a VPN or proxy and try again; if you can, try another network. If only updates fail for hours, wait – nothing on the PC needs changing.

wu.meaning: A version upgrade was started and rolled back. Microsoft calls this a generic rollback code that usually points to a device driver that does not work with the new version; the second code after the dash on screen names the phase in which it happened.
wu.next: Unplug everything except mouse, keyboard and screen, install current drivers from the PC maker and pending normal updates, free up space and try again.

wu.meaning: The PC does not meet the minimum requirements of the Windows version it was offered.
wu.next: Compare the PC with Microsoft’s published requirements. If it falls short, this upgrade is not for this PC – no setting changes that.

wu.meaning: Leftovers of an earlier upgrade attempt still wait to be cleaned up.
wu.next: Restart and start the upgrade again. If it repeats, Microsoft’s page describes removing temporary and system files with Windows’ own Disk Cleanup.

wu.meaning: An installed program is not compatible with the new Windows version and blocks the upgrade.
wu.next: Update or uninstall the incompatible program, then start the upgrade again. Microsoft’s page explains how to identify it.

wu.meaning: There is not enough free disk space for the upgrade.
wu.next: Free up space with Windows’ own storage settings and try again; Microsoft’s page states how much the upgrade needs.

wu.meaning: The disk is full: there is not enough free space to install the update or upgrade.
wu.next: Free up space with Windows’ own storage settings and try again.

ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED.meaning: The name lookup (DNS) failed, so no connection to the website was even attempted. Either the address is misspelled or no longer exists, or the DNS server your network uses gave no usable answer. If other sites open, check the spelling first, then test the DNS server.

ERR_INTERNET_DISCONNECTED.meaning: Chrome sees no network connection on this device. The website, your provider and the internet at large were never asked – the cause sits between this device and the router.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT.meaning: The name was found, a connection was tried and nobody answered in time. DNS is not the problem. Either the server is down or overloaded, or something on the way silently drops the traffic – a firewall, a VPN or a filter. The comparison with mobile data separates the two.

ERR_TIMED_OUT.meaning: An operation ran out of time without an answer. For a web page that means the same as a connection timeout: the server or the path to it did not respond. Compare with mobile data to see which side it follows.

ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED.meaning: Something at that address answered and actively refused the connection. That is different from a timeout: the path works. It fits a server whose web service is not running, an address with a wrong port, or a firewall that rejects instead of ignoring.

ERR_CONNECTION_RESET.meaning: A connection existed and was cut off. The cut can come from the server or from anything in between that inspects traffic – security software, a company or hotel filter, a VPN. If the site opens on mobile data, look at your own network and device.

ERR_CONNECTION_CLOSED.meaning: The other side closed the connection before sending a page. As with a reset, the server or a device in between ended it; compare with another network and another browser.

ERR_CONNECTION_ABORTED.meaning: The connection was given up because the other side did not confirm data in time. It points to an unstable path – weak Wi-Fi, a struggling router or a server in trouble – rather than to a wrong setting.

ERR_CONNECTION_FAILED.meaning: The connection attempt failed without a more specific reason. On its own it does not name a layer; the comparison checks (other sites, mobile data, another browser) have to.

ERR_ADDRESS_UNREACHABLE.meaning: The device knows the server’s address but has no route to it. That is a network-level fault: the router, the provider or a VPN – not the browser and usually not the website.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

ERR_NETWORK_CHANGED.meaning: The device’s network changed while the page was loading – a switch between Wi-Fi, cable and mobile data, a VPN connecting, or a new address from the router. Reload once. If it keeps coming back, the Wi-Fi link or the VPN is unstable.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT.meaning: Something inside the browser blocked the request – in practice an extension such as a content blocker. The network and the website are not involved. A private window, where extensions are normally off, shows it at once.

ERR_BLOCKED_BY_ADMINISTRATOR.meaning: A policy set by whoever manages this browser or device blocks the address. On a work or school device that is IT’s decision; on a private device, check whether the browser says it is “managed” and by whom.

ERR_NETWORK_ACCESS_DENIED.meaning: The browser was not allowed to use the network. Chromium’s own note says this is most likely a firewall – look at the firewall or security software on this device, not at the router.

ERR_PROXY_CONNECTION_FAILED.meaning: The browser is set to use a proxy server and could not reach it. The website never saw the request. Check the proxy setting of the system or of a VPN or security app that installed one.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED.meaning: A connection through a proxy could not be set up. As with other proxy errors, the place to look is the proxy or VPN configured on this device or network.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS.meaning: The site sent the browser from address to address in a circle. Either the website is misconfigured or a cookie it stored in your browser no longer fits. A private window tells the two apart.

ERR_EMPTY_RESPONSE.meaning: The server accepted the connection and closed it without sending anything. That is the server’s or an in-between filter’s doing, not a setting in your browser.

ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR.meaning: Browser and server could not set up the encrypted connection. Do not look for a way round it. Test another device and another network to see whether it follows the website or your side – security software that inspects encrypted traffic can cause it.

ERR_SSL_VERSION_OR_CIPHER_MISMATCH.meaning: Browser and server have no encryption method in common. That is decided by the server’s configuration or by software that inspects encrypted traffic; nothing on a normal home device needs changing.

ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID.meaning: By your device’s clock the site’s certificate is expired or not yet valid. Chromium lists three possible reasons: an attacker with an old certificate, a misconfigured server – or a wrong clock on your device. Check date, time and time zone first; do not click through.

ERR_HTTP_RESPONSE_CODE_FAILURE.meaning: The server answered, but with an HTTP error status. The connection and DNS are fine; the status code (404, 500, 503 …) says more.

ERR_HTTP2_PROTOCOL_ERROR.meaning: An error inside the HTTP/2 conversation with the server. Usually the website’s side or a device in between; test another network and another browser before changing anything.

ERR_QUIC_PROTOCOL_ERROR.meaning: An error in QUIC, the transport Chrome uses for HTTP/3. Usually the website’s side or a network that handles QUIC badly; test another network and another browser.

ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND.meaning: A file on this device was not found – as with an address that starts with file://. No network layer is involved.

ERR_INVALID_URL.meaning: The address itself is not a valid URL. Check for a typing mistake, a stray space or a missing part.

ERR_UNSAFE_PORT.meaning: The address contains a port number that Chrome refuses to connect to for web pages. That is the browser’s own safety rule, not a network fault.

ERR_DNS_TIMED_OUT.meaning: The DNS server did not answer in time. The website was never contacted; the fault is between this device and the DNS server – router, provider or a DNS setting on the device.

ERR_DNS_SERVER_FAILURE.meaning: The DNS server answered with a failure. The website was never contacted; test another DNS server to see whether your network’s DNS is the problem.

System.meaning: A general or local error – files, memory, permissions or a cancelled request. On its own it does not point to the router, the provider or the website.

Connection.meaning: The connection to the server or to a proxy failed at network or encryption level. Compare with another website and with mobile data to see whether it follows the website or your network.

Certificate.meaning: A certificate error: the browser could not confirm that the site is the one it claims to be. Do not click through and do not type passwords or card numbers. Check the date and time on your device, then try the site later or from another network; if the warning stays, only the website’s owner can fix it.

HTTP.meaning: A problem in the HTTP exchange with the server – the connection itself worked. Most of these can only be fixed by the website; a private window shows whether your browser data plays a part.

Cache.meaning: Concerns Chrome’s local cache of earlier downloads, not the network.

DNS resolver.meaning: The name lookup failed. The website was never contacted; the fault is on the way to the DNS server or at the DNS server.

Certificate manager.meaning: Concerns importing or managing certificates in the browser, not loading a normal web page.

Blob.meaning: Concerns data the page handles inside the browser, not the network.

Unnamed range.meaning: Chromium’s list gives this range no name.

DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN.meaning: Chrome ran its own DNS test: the DNS servers work, so the name does not exist. Check the spelling of the address. If it is right, the site’s domain may have lapsed – or a filter on your network answers “no such name” on purpose.

DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NO_INTERNET.meaning: Chrome’s DNS test found no internet connection at all. Start with the connection, not with the website.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_BAD_CONFIG.meaning: Chrome’s DNS test says the DNS settings are wrong or the DNS servers are down. Look for a manual DNS entry or a VPN on this device, then at the router.

DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_BAD_SECURE_CONFIG.meaning: Chrome’s DNS test failed with the secure DNS (DNS over HTTPS) provider set in Chrome. The network’s normal DNS may be fine – check Chrome’s secure DNS setting.

DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_INCONCLUSIVE.meaning: Chrome’s DNS test reached no conclusion. Use the comparison checks instead.

DNS_PROBE_STARTED.meaning: Chrome is still testing DNS; the code on the page changes when the test has finished. Wait a few seconds.

DNS_PROBE_POSSIBLE.meaning: Chrome has not run its DNS test yet; the code on the page changes when it has.

DNS_PROBE_NOT_RUN.meaning: Chrome did not run its DNS test, so the code says nothing about the cause.

100.meaning: An interim answer: the server has seen the start of the request and the browser may send the rest. You never see it as an error.

101.meaning: The server agrees to switch to another protocol on this connection, for example for a live chat channel. Not an error.

200.meaning: The request worked and the page was delivered. If it still looks broken, the cause is in the page itself or in the browser (extensions, stored data), not in the transfer.

204.meaning: The request worked and the server has nothing to show for it. Normal after saving something in a web app.

206.meaning: The server delivered a requested part of a file – normal when a download is resumed or a video is skipped forward.

301.meaning: The address has moved for good; browsers follow automatically. You only notice it when redirects run in a circle.

302.meaning: A temporary redirect; browsers follow automatically. You only notice it when redirects run in a circle.

303.meaning: After a form was sent, the server points the browser to a result page. Normal behaviour.

304.meaning: Not an error: the server confirms that the copy your browser already stored is still current.

307.meaning: A temporary redirect that keeps the kind of request unchanged. Browsers follow automatically.

308.meaning: A permanent redirect that keeps the kind of request unchanged. Browsers follow automatically.

400.meaning: The server rejected the request as malformed. From a browser, data stored for that site (cookies) can be the cause: test a private window, then clear that one site’s data.

401.meaning: The server wants a valid sign-in for this address. Sign in again; if the page belongs to a company or school, the account needs access.

403.meaning: The server understood the request and refuses it. Your connection works. The site decides this – by account, by country or by the address you come from, for example when you use a VPN.

404.meaning: The server is up but has nothing at this exact address. Check the spelling after the domain name; an old link or bookmark is the usual reason. Nothing on your device needs fixing.

405.meaning: The page exists but does not accept this kind of request – for example a form sent to an address that only shows pages. A fault in the website or in an outdated bookmark to a form step.

407.meaning: The exception among the 4xx codes: this answer comes from a proxy between you and the website, not from the website. The proxy wants a sign-in. On a company or school network ask IT; on a private device check whether a proxy or a VPN app is set that should not be.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

408.meaning: The server gave up waiting for the browser’s request. Reload once; if it repeats on a slow or unstable connection, look at the Wi-Fi link.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

409.meaning: The request collides with the current state on the server – typically two people or two tabs changed the same thing. Reload the page and repeat the change.

410.meaning: The page was removed on purpose and is not coming back at this address.

413.meaning: What you tried to send is larger than the server accepts – usually an upload. Make the file smaller; nothing is wrong with your connection.

414.meaning: The address itself is too long for the server. This happens with links that carry a lot of data after the question mark; open the site from its start page instead.

415.meaning: The server does not accept the format of what was sent – for example an upload in a file type the site does not support.

421.meaning: The request reached a server that is not responsible for this address. A fault in the website’s setup or in a connection the browser reused; closing and reopening the browser makes it connect afresh.

426.meaning: The server insists on a newer protocol than the one used. Seen with very old browsers or apps: update the browser.

428.meaning: The server only accepts the change with a safeguard against overwriting someone else’s edit. A matter for the web app; reload and try again.

429.meaning: Too many requests from your address or account in a short time. Wait – every reload adds another request. On a shared network or VPN, the limit is shared with others.

431.meaning: The browser sent more header data than the server accepts – for example too many or too large cookies for that site. Test a private window, then clear that one site’s cookies.

451.meaning: The site withholds the page for legal reasons, typically depending on the country you connect from. Nothing is broken on your side.

500.meaning: The website’s server ran into an error of its own. Only the site can fix it; try again later or check its status page.

501.meaning: The server does not support what the request asked it to do. A fault in the website or app, not on your device.

502.meaning: A server in front of the website (gateway or proxy) got an invalid answer from the server behind it. A problem inside the website’s infrastructure – wait and retry.

503.meaning: The server is temporarily overloaded or down for maintenance. Wait and retry; a status page often confirms it.

504.meaning: A gateway in front of the website waited too long for the server behind it. As with 502, the website’s side.

505.meaning: The server does not support the HTTP version the request used. A server or app fault; a current browser does not cause it.

511.meaning: The second exception: this answer comes from the network you are on, not from the website. The network wants you to sign in first – the sign-in page of a hotel, café, train or guest Wi-Fi. Open a plain address in a new tab to get the sign-in page; until then nothing else will load.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

1.meaning: Informational: an interim answer while the request continues. Not an error.

2.meaning: Successful: the server did what was asked. If the page still looks wrong, the cause is in the page or the browser, not in the transfer.

3.meaning: Redirection: the browser is sent to another address and normally follows without showing anything.

4.meaning: Client error class: the server answered and says the request cannot be fulfilled as sent. Your connection, DNS and the server all work; check the address, your sign-in and the site’s data in your browser.

5.meaning: Server error class: the server answered and says it failed. Your device and network work; only the website can fix it.

169.254.0.0/16.meaning: A link-local address: the device gave it to itself because no DHCP server – normally your router – answered. With such an address the device can reach neither the router nor the internet. The fault is in the link between this device and the router, not at the provider or the website.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

Private-Use.meaning: A private address, as a home or office router hands out. It shows that the device is joined to the network and received an address, so the device–router link works at this level. Private addresses are not visible from the internet; many devices worldwide use the same ones.

next.label: Diagnosis: Wi-Fi connected but no internet

100.64.0.0/10.meaning: Shared address space, reserved for the link between a customer’s router and the provider when the provider uses carrier-grade NAT. If your router shows such an address as its internet (WAN) address, you share a public address with other customers: browsing works, but port forwarding from the internet to your home cannot.

127.0.0.0/8.meaning: A loopback address: it always means “this device itself”. A page or tool using it talks to software on the same computer, never to the network.

0.0.0.0/8.meaning: An address a device uses for itself before it has a real one. Shown as the device’s address, it means no address has been assigned yet.

0.0.0.0/32.meaning: The placeholder for “this host” before an address is assigned. Shown as the device’s address, it means it has none yet.

255.255.255.255/32.meaning: The limited broadcast address: “everyone on this local network”. Never the address of a single device.

224.0.0.0/4.meaning: A multicast address: used to reach a group of devices at once, for example when devices look for printers on the local network. Never the address of a single device.

ff00::/8.meaning: An IPv6 multicast address: used to reach a group of devices at once. Never the address of a single device.

fe80::/10.meaning: An IPv6 link-local address. Every IPv6 device has one and it only works inside the local network, so it is normal to see it next to other addresses. If it is the only IPv6 address, the network offers no IPv6 internet access – IPv4 may still work.

fc00::/7.meaning: An IPv6 unique local address: the IPv6 counterpart of a private address. It works inside your network and is not reachable from the internet.

::1/128.meaning: The IPv6 loopback address: “this device itself”.

::/128.meaning: The unspecified IPv6 address: a device without an address yet.

Documentation.meaning: A range reserved for examples in manuals and documentation. A real device should never have it – if you copied it from instructions, replace it with your own value.

publicV4.meaning: A public IPv4 address. Behind a home router a device normally shows a private address instead; a public one means the device is connected directly to the modem or to the provider’s network, without a router in between. As the router’s internet (WAN) address it is the normal case.

publicV6.meaning: A public (global) IPv6 address. Unlike IPv4, it is normal for every device at home to have one: IPv6 does not need private addresses and address translation.
